_comment: Supplemental items, PN batch 03: Coordinated Care. Pilot status.

questions.stem: The LPN/VN in a family practice clinic is reviewing phone messages to route to the RN and provider. Which message needs the quickest follow-up?
questions.rationale: A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in an infant younger than 3 months can signal a serious bacterial infection and needs same-day, urgent evaluation. A refill request, a question about returning to preschool after a cold, and rescheduling a physical are routine.

options.text: A client asks whether the clinic can send a refill of a blood pressure medicine
A parent asks whether a 4-year-old can return to preschool after a cold
A client wants to move a routine physical to a different week
A parent reports that their 6-week-old infant has a temperature of 100.6°F (38.1°C)

questions.stem: The LPN/VN on a surgical unit is collecting data on four clients. Which finding should the LPN/VN report to the RN immediately?
questions.rationale: Sudden dyspnea and chest pain after orthopedic surgery suggest a pulmonary embolism, a life-threatening emergency. Tolerable pain, mild nausea when starting a diet, and a request for help to the bathroom can be addressed after the emergency is reported.

options.text: Incisional pain of 3/10 that the client rates as tolerable 1 day after a laparoscopic appendectomy
Sudden shortness of breath and chest pain 3 days after a hip replacement
Mild nausea after the first clear liquid meal
A request for help to the bathroom

questions.stem: The LPN/VN has just received report. Which client should the LPN/VN see first?
questions.rationale: Shakiness, sweating, and confusion in a client with diabetes suggest hypoglycemia, a physiological problem that can quickly worsen and must be treated first. Emotional distress about a delay, menu selection, and a shower are important but can wait briefly.

options.text: A client with diabetes who is shaky, sweaty, and confused before lunch
A client who is crying after learning that discharge will be delayed by a day
A client who wants help filling out a menu for tomorrow's meals and snacks
A client who wants a shower

questions.stem: The LPN/VN in an outpatient dialysis unit is collecting data on four clients. Which client should the LPN/VN report to the RN first?
questions.rationale: Chest pain during dialysis may signal myocardial ischemia from hypotension or fluid shifts, or another emergency, and needs immediate RN assessment. Fatigue after dialysis is common, and requests for a blanket or the dietitian are routine.

options.text: A client who reports feeling tired after the last three dialysis sessions
A client who asks for a blanket because the treatment area feels cold today
A client who develops chest pain during dialysis
A client who asks when the dietitian will be available to talk about meal plans

questions.stem: The family of a competent resident in long-term care asks the LPN/VN to stop putting through the resident's phone calls from a friend the family dislikes. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Residents in long-term care have the right to private communication with people of their choosing, including by phone. A competent resident's family cannot restrict that right, and staff should not secretly block calls or leave the decision to others. The LPN/VN can involve the RN or social worker if the family has safety concerns.

options.text: Explain that the resident has the right to communicate with people they choose
Block the friend's calls, since the family knows what is best
Ask the friend to stop calling the facility without telling the resident
Let the facility's receptionist decide whether to put the calls through

questions.stem: A resident in long-term care asks to keep their own inhaler at the bedside and use it without staff help. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Residents have the right to self-administer medications if the interdisciplinary team determines that it is clinically appropriate and safe. The LPN/VN reports the request so the assessment can be done. A blanket refusal ignores the resident's rights, and handing over the inhaler without an assessment and a prescription bypasses the process.

options.text: Tell the resident that all medications in long-term care must be given by staff, with no exceptions
Give the inhaler to the resident to keep
Report the request to the RN so the team can assess whether self-administration is safe
Refuse and document the request

questions.stem: A married couple asks the LPN/VN for private time together when the spouse visits a resident in long-term care. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Residents in long-term care have the right to privacy, including private visits with a spouse. The LPN/VN arranges a private space and makes sure staff respect it. Refusing privacy, frequent checks without a safety reason, and requiring visits in a public area violate the resident's rights.

options.text: Explain that facility rules do not allow residents to have private visits
Arrange privacy, such as a closed door with a do-not-disturb sign
Ask an assistive personnel to check on the couple every 10 minutes during the visit
Ask the couple to visit in the lounge

questions.stem: A 15-year-old who is not emancipated is scheduled for an elective knee repair. Who should sign the surgical consent?
questions.rationale: For most procedures, a minor who is not emancipated needs consent from a parent or legal guardian, although the teen should be included in the discussion and asked to agree. A surgeon cannot consent for the client, and other relatives cannot consent unless they are the legal guardian.

options.text: The 15-year-old, since the surgery is being done on the teen's own body
The surgeon, since the procedure is elective and was recommended by the surgeon
Any adult relative who comes to the hospital with the teen on the day of surgery
The parent or legal guardian

questions.stem: An unconscious adult with internal bleeding after a car crash needs emergency surgery, and no family can be reached. Which statement about consent is accurate?
questions.rationale: In a true emergency, when a client cannot consent and no surrogate is available, consent is implied for treatment needed to prevent death or serious harm. Waiting for family or a court order could cost the client's life, and nurses do not sign consent on a client's behalf.

options.text: Consent is implied, so the surgery can proceed to preserve the client's life and health
The surgery must wait until a family member can be found to sign the consent form
The LPN/VN can sign the consent form for the client, since the client is unconscious
A court order is required before any emergency surgery can begin

questions.stem: A client being admitted hands the LPN/VN a copy of their living will. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: An advance directive brought on admission is placed in the record and communicated to the RN and provider so the client's wishes guide care. Living wills apply in any care setting, a valid directive does not need to be redone on a facility form, and giving it to the family keeps it from the team.

options.text: Return it to the client, since living wills apply only when a client is in a nursing home
Ask the client to sign a new living will on the facility's own form
Make sure a copy goes into the record and tell the RN so the provider is aware
Give it to the family to keep

questions.stem: A resident asks the LPN/VN to sign as a witness on the resident's new will for their property. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Witnessing a legal document such as a property will is not part of nursing practice, and many facilities prohibit staff from doing it because of possible conflicts of interest. The LPN/VN follows policy, which often directs these requests to social services or the resident's attorney. Asking an AP to sign does not solve the problem, and nurses do not give legal advice.

options.text: Sign right away, since witnessing a will is one of the LPN/VN's legal duties
Follow facility policy, which usually refers the request to social services
Ask an assistive personnel on the unit to sign as the witness instead of the nurse
Read the will and advise the resident

questions.stem: The wound care protocol calls for weekly photographs of a resident's pressure injury. Which action by the LPN/VN is correct?
questions.rationale: Client photographs are protected health information. They are taken with facility-approved devices, with consent as policy requires, and stored only in the record. Personal phones and texting can expose images even after they are deleted, and group chats share them with people who do not need them.

options.text: Take the photo with a personal phone and delete it after uploading it to the record
Text the photo to the wound nurse from a personal phone so the nurse sees it sooner
Post the photo in the unit's group chat so all staff can follow how the wound is healing
Use the facility's approved device and follow its photo policy

questions.stem: A client taking several prescribed medications asks the LPN/VN whether it is safe to start taking St. John's wort. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Herbal supplements can interact with prescribed drugs; St. John's wort, for example, reduces the effect of many medications and can cause serotonin syndrome with some antidepressants. The LPN/VN refers the question to the pharmacist or provider. Natural products are not automatically safe, and starting or increasing a supplement without review can cause harm.

options.text: Tell the client that herbal supplements are natural and are safe with any medication
Advise checking with the pharmacist or provider, since herbs can interact with medications
Tell the client to start the supplement and stop it if any side effects develop
Suggest that the client take a double dose to see results faster

questions.topic: Following up on data from an AP
questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) reports normal vital signs for a resident, but when the LPN/VN walks by, the resident looks pale and sweaty. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: When data reported by an AP do not match what the nurse observes, the nurse checks the client personally. Pallor and sweating may signal hypoglycemia, hypotension, or another acute problem. Accepting readings that do not fit the client's appearance or waiting to recheck could delay needed care.

options.text: Accept the AP's readings, since the AP is trained to take vital signs and recorded them correctly
Ask the AP to recheck later
Document the AP's readings
Check the resident and recheck the vital signs personally

questions.stem: The LPN/VN sees an assistive personnel (AP) walking an unsteady resident without a gait belt. What should the LPN/VN do first?
questions.rationale: The resident's immediate safety comes first, so the LPN/VN intervenes, steadies the resident, and has the AP use a gait belt. Feedback to the AP follows. Waiting or reporting before acting leaves the resident at risk of falling.

options.text: Wait until the walk is finished and then remind the AP about gait belts at the end of the shift
Report the AP to the director of nursing before saying anything to the AP
Help steady the resident and have the AP apply a gait belt
Let the walk continue

questions.topic: Reviewing the need for a urinary catheter
questions.stem: A client has had an indwelling urinary catheter since surgery 4 days ago, is now walking to the bathroom with help, and has no documented reason for the catheter. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: The risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection rises each day a catheter stays in, so evidence-based practice calls for daily review and prompt removal when it is no longer indicated. The LPN/VN raises the question with the RN so the provider or protocol can authorize removal. Convenience is not an indication, removal requires a prescription or protocol, and clamping is not recommended routinely.

options.text: Ask the RN whether the catheter is still needed
Leave the catheter in place until the client is discharged, since it is more convenient for staff
Remove the catheter without a prescription because it is no longer needed
Clamp the catheter for several hours to retrain the bladder before discharge

questions.topic: Finding client information in a public area
questions.stem: The LPN/VN finds another nurse's printed report sheet with client names and diagnoses on a table in the hospital cafeteria. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Client information left in a public place is a privacy breach. The LPN/VN secures the sheet right away, returns it or shreds it according to policy, and reports the incident so the facility can respond as required. Leaving it exposes the information, regular trash is not secure, and reading more than needed adds to the breach.

options.text: Leave the sheet on the table, since the nurse who wrote it will probably come back for it
Throw the sheet in the cafeteria trash can so that no one else picks it up
Read the sheet to find out which unit it came from and return it later
Secure the sheet and return it to the unit or dispose of it per policy, and report the breach

questions.stem: A visitor asks the LPN/VN for a client's room number. The client asked on admission not to be listed in the facility directory. What should the LPN/VN say?
questions.rationale: When a client opts out of the facility directory, staff do not confirm that the client is present or give a location. A response that neither confirms nor denies protects the client's privacy. Giving the room number, going to ask the client, or telling the visitor to wait would confirm that the client is there.

options.text: "The client is in room 214, but please don't tell anyone that I gave you the room number."
"I'm sorry, I'm not able to give out any information about that person."
"Let me check with the client."
"Wait here for the client."

questions.topic: Family request to withhold a diagnosis
questions.stem: The family of a competent client asks the LPN/VN not to tell the client about a new diagnosis of cancer. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: A competent client has the right to information about their own health and to decide how much they want to know. The LPN/VN informs the RN and provider so they can learn the client's preferences and address the family's concerns. Keeping the diagnosis secret at the family's request violates the client's rights, and delivering a new diagnosis is the provider's role.

options.text: Notify the RN and provider so the client's wishes about information can be clarified
Agree to keep the diagnosis from the client, since the family knows the client best of all
Tell the client the diagnosis immediately, before the provider can discuss it with them
Change the subject

questions.topic: Request for a caregiver of the same gender
questions.stem: A client tells the LPN/VN that, because of religious beliefs, they want only female staff to help with bathing. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Respecting cultural and religious preferences about personal care is part of client-centered care, so the LPN/VN arranges same-gender caregivers when staffing allows and communicates the preference to the team. Refusing to consider it, withholding care, or requiring the client to justify the request is disrespectful. In an emergency, needed care is not delayed.

options.text: Explain that staff assignments are based on the schedule and cannot be changed for personal reasons
Tell the client that bathing will be skipped until the client accepts any staff member who is available
Arrange female staff for personal care when possible
Ask the client to explain the religious beliefs in detail first

questions.stem: A client tells the LPN/VN that they want to make a formal complaint about how they were treated in the emergency department. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Clients have the right to voice complaints and to have them reviewed. The LPN/VN listens and helps the client use the facility's grievance process, often through a patient advocate or relations office, without retaliation. Refusing, discouraging, or dismissing the complaint violates the client's rights.

options.text: Listen to the concern and explain how to file a grievance through the facility's process
Tell the client that complaints about another department cannot be taken here
Discourage the complaint, since it could make the staff feel uncomfortable
Tell the client the treatment was probably justified

questions.stem: The LPN/VN is caring for a client with a new colostomy and an assistive personnel (AP) is available. Which task should the LPN/VN perform rather than delegate?
questions.rationale: Reinforcing teaching and evaluating the client's understanding require nursing knowledge and judgment and stay with the licensed nurse. Emptying a stable ostomy pouch and measuring output, helping a stable client walk, and changing linens are routine tasks that can be delegated to an AP.

options.text: Emptying the pouch, measuring the stool output, and recording the amount in the chart
Helping the client walk in the hallway
Changing the bed linens
Reinforcing teaching about pouch changes and checking the client's understanding

questions.stem: The laboratory calls the LPN/VN with a critical potassium value of 6.8 mEq/L for a client. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: Critical results must be communicated to the responsible provider promptly. The nurse who receives the call writes down and reads back the result to confirm it and then reports it right away. A potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L can cause fatal dysrhythmias, so delays are dangerous, and the LPN/VN cannot order a new test.

options.text: Write the result on a sticky note and give it to the RN at the next break
Wait for the result to appear in the record before taking action
Read the result back and notify the RN and provider immediately
Recheck the potassium level

questions.stem: Near the end of the shift, the LPN/VN realizes they forgot to report a resident's new ankle swelling noticed that morning. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: The nurse is accountable for reporting findings. Reporting late is better than not reporting, so the LPN/VN reports now and documents accurately with the actual time. Assuming others will notice, back-timing an entry to suggest it was reported earlier, and waiting are all unsafe or dishonest.

options.text: Leave the finding out of the report, since the next shift will notice the swelling on its own
Report it to the RN now and document it accurately
Document the swelling with the morning time and say it was reported then
Wait until tomorrow to see whether the swelling goes away on its own

questions.stem: A client who must choose between surgery and radiation therapy asks the LPN/VN, "What would you do if you were me?" What is the LPN/VN's best response?
questions.rationale: The nurse supports the client's decision-making by helping the client explore their own values and priorities and by making sure the provider answers remaining questions. Giving a personal recommendation can unduly influence the client, deferring to the family does not respect the client's autonomy, and refusing to talk leaves the client without support.

options.text: "If I were you, I would choose the surgery, since it is the faster way to be finished with this."
"You should do whatever your family thinks is best for you."
"I'm not allowed to talk about it."
"What matters most to you as you think about each choice? I can let your provider know you have questions."

questions.stem: While completing a preoperative checklist, the LPN/VN finds that the surgical consent form has not been signed. The transport staff has arrived. What should the LPN/VN do?
questions.rationale: A required signed consent must be in place before an elective procedure. The LPN/VN stops the transfer and reports to the RN so the surgeon can obtain consent; the nurse does not obtain it. Sending the client without it risks proceeding without valid consent, and a family member cannot sign for a competent adult.

options.text: Hold the transport and report the missing consent to the RN right away
Send the client to surgery and tell the surgeon to obtain the consent in the preoperative holding area
Have the client sign the form now
Have a family member sign

questions.stem: At the same moment, a provider calls back about a resident's low blood pressure, a visitor at the desk asks for an update, and a resident's call light comes on for a fresh water pitcher. What should the LPN/VN do first?
questions.rationale: The provider's call concerns a possibly unstable resident and allows treatment decisions to be made, so it comes first. A request for water can be handled by an AP or right after the call, and the visitor can be asked to wait briefly. A visitor cannot take a clinical call.

options.text: Answer the call light first, since call lights must always be answered before anything else
Talk with the visitor first, since the visitor is standing at the desk
Take the provider's call about the resident's blood pressure
Ask the visitor to answer the phone

questions.stem: Which actions protect client information when the LPN/VN uses mobile devices at work? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Approved secure apps, passcodes, logging out, and keeping client information off personal devices protect privacy. Texting client names to personal phones and photographing records create unsecured copies of protected information.

options.text: Using only facility-approved apps for client communication
Locking the device with a passcode
Keeping client information off personal phones
Texting client names to a coworker's personal phone
Taking a photo of the medication record to check later
Logging out of work apps when finished

questions.stem: Which actions show effective supervision of assistive personnel (AP) by the LPN/VN? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Supervision means monitoring delegated work, giving specific feedback, and being available for help. The nurse remains responsible for outcomes and cannot assume tasks were done. Deciding whether a change needs to be reported requires nursing judgment, so the AP reports all changes to the nurse.

options.text: Checking during the shift that delegated tasks are being done correctly
Giving specific feedback when a task is not done correctly
Being available to answer the AP's questions
Assuming tasks were done correctly unless a resident complains
Letting the AP decide whether a change in a resident should be reported

questions.stem: A client refuses a prescribed dressing change. What should the LPN/VN include in the documentation? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Documentation of a refusal includes what was refused, the client's stated reason, the education provided about risks, and who was notified, such as the RN and provider. Personal judgments about the client's character are not objective and do not belong in the record.

options.text: The care that was refused
The reason the client gave, in the client's words
The information given to the client about the risks of refusing
Who was notified of the refusal
The LPN/VN's opinion that the client is being difficult

questions.topic: Situations that require an event report
questions.stem: Which situations require the LPN/VN to complete an event (incident) report? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Event reports are completed for falls, medication errors, injuries to visitors, and equipment failures that affect safety, so the facility can analyze and prevent them. A client's choice to decline an activity or change a meal is documented as needed but is not an adverse event.

options.text: A resident falls in the bathroom
A client receives a dose of medication intended for another client
A visitor slips on a wet floor and injures a wrist
A malfunctioning bed alarm fails to sound when a resident gets up
A client refuses an afternoon walk
A client asks for a different meal

questions.stem: Which actions by the LPN/VN demonstrate client advocacy? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Advocacy means protecting the client's rights and interests: making sure the client can communicate, that symptoms are addressed, and that informed decisions are respected. Pressuring a client on behalf of others or deciding for a client who is able to decide undermines autonomy.

options.text: Requesting a medical interpreter for a client with limited English
Reporting a client's unrelieved pain to the RN
Supporting a competent client's decision to decline a treatment
Persuading a client to accept a procedure the family wants
Making decisions for a client who seems unsure

questions.topic: Prioritizing by airway, breathing, and circulation
questions.stem: After report, which clients need the LPN/VN's immediate attention and a report to the RN? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Stridor threatens the airway, new slurred speech may signal a stroke, and severe hypotension threatens circulation; these need immediate attention. Moderate pain, a snack request, and a bath can be handled after the emergencies.

options.text: A client with new stridor after a meal
A client with a new onset of slurred speech
A client whose blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg
A client with incisional pain of 4/10
A client who asks for a snack
A client who wants a bath before visitors arrive

questions.topic: Continuity at the end of a shift
questions.stem: Which actions by the LPN/VN at the end of a shift support continuity of care? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Complete documentation, a report of pending items and changes, and leaving clients safe at handoff help the next nurse continue care without gaps. An unlocked medication cart is a safety risk, and controlled-substance keys must be counted and handed off, not taken home.

options.text: Completing documentation for care given during the shift
Reporting pending tests, results, and tasks to the oncoming nurse
Making sure each client's call light is within reach
Sharing any changes in condition during handoff
Leaving the medication cart unlocked for the next nurse
Taking the controlled-substance keys home by mistake

questions.stem: For each situation, indicate whom the LPN/VN should contact.
questions.rationale: Changes in a resident's condition, such as new chest pressure or sudden confusion, go to the RN for assessment. Pharmacists answer questions about medication preparation and interactions. Broken equipment is reported to biomedical or maintenance staff and taken out of use, and social workers help with financial and community resources.

rows.text: A resident's bed alarm will not turn on
A question about whether a tablet can be crushed
A resident reports new chest pressure
A resident is worried about paying for care
A question about an interaction between two prescribed drugs
A resident has a new, sudden change in mental status

questions.answer_summary: A resident's bed alarm will not turn on: Biomedical or maintenance staff; A question about whether a tablet can be crushed: Pharmacist; A resident reports new chest pressure: RN; A resident is worried about paying for care: Social worker; A question about an interaction between two prescribed drugs: Pharmacist; A resident has a new, sudden change in mental status: RN

questions.stem: For each situation, indicate whether the consent is valid or not valid.
questions.rationale: Valid consent requires a competent person with legal authority, adequate information, understanding, and a voluntary decision. A sedated client, a minor who is not emancipated, and a client who could not understand the information cannot give valid consent. A legal guardian may consent for a client who lacks capacity, and an emancipated minor may consent for their own care.

rows.text: A competent adult signs after the surgeon explains the procedure, risks, and alternatives
A client signs 15 minutes after receiving IV morphine and is drowsy
A 15-year-old who is not emancipated signs for an elective surgery
A court-appointed guardian signs for a client with severe dementia
A client who reads only Spanish signs an English form without an interpreter
An emancipated 17-year-old signs for their own surgery

questions.answer_summary: A competent adult signs after the surgeon explains the procedure, risks, and alternatives: Valid; A client signs 15 minutes after receiving IV morphine and is drowsy: Not valid; A 15-year-old who is not emancipated signs for an elective surgery: Not valid; A court-appointed guardian signs for a client with severe dementia: Valid; A client who reads only Spanish signs an English form without an interpreter: Not valid; An emancipated 17-year-old signs for their own surgery: Valid

questions.stem: For each task, indicate whether the LPN/VN should delegate it to an assistive personnel (AP) or do it personally.
questions.rationale: Routine tasks with predictable outcomes for stable residents, such as walking, bed making, and measuring intake and output, can be delegated. Reinforcing teaching, collecting data on a new problem, and checking a resident with a new symptom require nursing knowledge and judgment.

rows.text: Walking a stable resident to the dining room
Reinforcing teaching about using an inhaler
Collecting data on a new skin tear
Making an occupied bed
Measuring and recording intake and output
Checking a resident who reports new chest discomfort

questions.answer_summary: Walking a stable resident to the dining room: Delegate to AP; Reinforcing teaching about using an inhaler: LPN/VN does it; Collecting data on a new skin tear: LPN/VN does it; Making an occupied bed: Delegate to AP; Measuring and recording intake and output: Delegate to AP; Checking a resident who reports new chest discomfort: LPN/VN does it

questions.topic: Transfer from long-term care to the hospital
questions.stem: A resident is being transferred from long-term care to the hospital. For each item, indicate whether it should be included in the transfer information.
questions.rationale: Transfer information gives the receiving team what it needs for safe care: code status, medications with last dose times, the resident's baseline mental and functional status for comparison, and allergies. Entertainment preferences and the roommate's name do not affect acute care, and sharing a roommate's information is a privacy concern.

rows.text: Code status and advance directives
Current medications and the time of the last doses
The resident's usual mental status and level of function
Known allergies
The resident's favorite television programs
The name of the resident's roommate

questions.answer_summary: Code status and advance directives: Include; Current medications and the time of the last doses: Include; The resident's usual mental status and level of function: Include; Known allergies: Include; The resident's favorite television programs: Not needed; The name of the resident's roommate: Not needed

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease tells the LPN/VN, "I've decided to stop dialysis. I know I will probably die within a few weeks, and I'm ready." The client is alert and oriented, has said the same thing consistently for a month, and scored in the normal range on a recent depression screening. Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the situation most likely represents, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters the LPN/VN should monitor.
questions.rationale: The client is alert, oriented, consistent over time, aware of the consequences, and has no signs of depression or delirium, so this is an informed refusal by a competent client. The LPN/VN notifies the RN and provider so the decision and the client's goals can be discussed and documented, and offers palliative and spiritual support. Pressuring the client, scheduling treatment anyway, or saying refusal is not allowed violates the client's rights. As kidney failure progresses, fluid overload causes shortness of breath and swelling, and comfort and pain guide symptom management.

bowtie_groups.label: Condition (choose 1)
options: Informed refusal of treatment by a competent client
Lack of understanding of the consequences

bowtie_groups.label: Actions to take (choose 2)
options: Notify the RN and provider so the decision can be discussed and documented
Ask whether the client would like a palliative care or chaplain visit
Ask the family to convince the client to continue dialysis
Schedule the next dialysis session anyway
Tell the client that stopping dialysis is not allowed

questions.answer_summary: Condition: Informed refusal of treatment by a competent client. Actions: Notify the RN and provider so the decision can be discussed and documented; Ask whether the client would like a palliative care or chaplain visit. Monitor: Shortness of breath and swelling; Comfort and pain level.

questions.topic: Missed care from an overloaded AP
questions.stem: At 1200, the LPN/VN finds that a resident who needs full help with care has an untouched breakfast tray, a wet brief, and has not been repositioned since 0600. The assigned assistive personnel (AP) has 14 residents today because another AP called in sick and says, "I can't keep up." Complete the diagram by choosing the condition the situation most likely represents, 2 actions the LPN/VN should take, and 2 parameters the LPN/VN should monitor.
questions.rationale: The AP has an unusually heavy assignment and reports being unable to keep up, so the missed care reflects an unsafe workload rather than refusal, expected decline, or intentional neglect. The LPN/VN first makes sure the resident receives the missed care and then reports the staffing problem so assignments can be redistributed. Disciplining the AP first, waiting for the next shift, and complaining to the family do not meet the resident's needs. Skin over pressure points and food and fluid intake show whether the missed repositioning and meal caused harm.

bowtie_groups.label: Condition (choose 1)
options: Missed care because of an unsafe workload

bowtie_groups.label: Actions to take (choose 2)
options: Provide or arrange the missed care for the resident right away
Report the workload to the supervisor so assignments can be adjusted
Write up the AP for poor performance before helping the resident
Wait for the next shift to catch up on the care
Tell the family that the facility is short-staffed today

questions.answer_summary: Condition: Missed care because of an unsafe workload. Actions: Provide or arrange the missed care for the resident right away; Report the workload to the supervisor so assignments can be adjusted. Monitor: Skin over pressure points; Food and fluid intake.
